overview.title: AGI hype, cognitive automation vs. intelligence
overview.main_topic: Why claims of imminent AGI deserve skepticism, and the distinction between cognitive automation (what today's AI is) and intelligence (cognitive autonomy)
overview.central_idea: Today's 'artificial intelligence' is better described as cognitive automation — the encoding and operationalization of human skills — and it is adaptability to the genuinely unknown, not realism of output, that separates automation from intelligence. Historically, belief in near-term AGI preceded and helped fuel generative AI, not the other way round.
overview.importance: This page sets the intellectual stance of the whole book: enthusiasm for the practical power of deep learning combined with a sober view of its limits. The 'cartoon vs. living being' distinction and the definition of intelligence as the ability to face, adapt to and learn from the unknown return in chapter 19 (p.600, p.603) when the authors discuss what is still missing on the road to real intelligence.
learning_objectives: Recount the authors' historical argument that belief in near-term AGI (c. 2013–2016) contributed to the founding of OpenAI and hence to generative AI, rather than being caused by it.
Explain why the authors prefer the term 'cognitive automation' to 'artificial intelligence' for today's systems.
Distinguish cognitive automation from intelligence (cognitive autonomy) using the cartoon-character vs. living-being analogy.
State the authors' criterion for intelligence — adaptability to the unknown — and why it makes robust automation hard to build.
prerequisites: The definitions of AI, machine learning and deep learning from section 1.1–1.3 (p.26–27)
The list of deep-learning achievements in section 1.9 (p.35–36), which is what the hype is built on
The opening of section 1.10 on p.36 (hype about the economy and productivity)

summary:
This page continues section 1.10, *Beware of the short-term hype*. After finishing the thought from p.36 — that the realistic economic impact of AI pales next to the "unbridled promises" made at its onset — the authors turn to the most sensational part of the hype: claims that human-level **artificial general intelligence (AGI)** or even "superintelligence" is imminent, and that humanity might be replaced by its digital creations.

The authors then make a historical point that newcomers usually get backwards. It is tempting to think the practical successes of generative AI *caused* the belief in near-term AGI. In fact the belief came **first**: as early as 2013 some tech elites feared that DeepMind (a London startup acquired by Google) was on track to AGI within a few years; that fear was the impetus for founding **OpenAI in 2015** as an open-source counterweight; OpenAI then played a critical role in kick-starting generative AI. In 2016 OpenAI's recruiting pitch was that it would achieve AGI by 2020. Only a minority believed such timelines then, but by early 2023 a significant fraction of Bay Area engineers expected AGI within a couple of years.

The authors urge skepticism. Despite its name, today's "artificial intelligence" is more accurately **cognitive automation**: the encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge. It excels at problems with narrowly defined requirements or with ample precise examples; it enhances computers rather than replicating minds. Cognitive automation is extremely useful, but **intelligence — cognitive autonomy — is a different creature**. The analogy: AI is a cartoon character that can only act out the scenes it was drawn for; intelligence is a living being that can adapt to the unexpected.

Anticipating the objection "if the cartoon covers enough scenes, what's the difference?" (or: if an LLM sounds human enough, does cognitive autonomy matter?), the authors answer: **adaptability**. Intelligence is the ability to face the unknown, adapt to it and learn from it; automation can only handle situations it was trained or programmed for — which is exactly why robust automation is so hard, since every scenario must be accounted for. Hence there is no reason to fear AI suddenly becoming self-aware: the technology is simply not headed that way. The sentence continues on p.38 with the clock-vs-time-travel comparison.

paragraphs.excerpt: overall economy and pales in comparison to the absolutely unbridled promises
paragraphs.what_it_says: This is the end of a sentence that started on p.36: the real impact of AI on the overall economy has been modest so far and pales in comparison to the unbridled promises made when the hype began.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The authors are contrasting measurable economic effect with the rhetoric that accompanied the launch of the generative-AI wave. The point is not that AI is useless (section 1.9 just listed its achievements) but that the gap between promise and delivery is large.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames the whole section: the problem being discussed is *over-promising*, which — as section 1.11 will explain on p.38 — historically leads to AI winters when expectations are not met.
connections: p.36: the sentence begins at the end of the previous page, in the opening of section 1.10.
p.38: section 1.11 describes what happens when inflated expectations fail — funding dries up.

paragraphs.excerpt: While discussions about unemployment and 100× productivity gains triggered by AI
paragraphs.what_it_says: Beyond anxieties about unemployment and 100× productivity gains, there is a more sensational strand of hype: the claim that human-level AGI, or a superintelligence far beyond humans, is imminent — and with it the fear that humanity could be replaced by its own digital creations.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The authors separate two layers of hype. The first (economic disruption) is at least about plausible effects of automation. The second (AGI / superintelligence / existential replacement) is a qualitatively stronger claim about the *nature* of the technology, not just its economic effect.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is this second layer that the rest of the page dismantles, by arguing that current systems are automation, not autonomous intelligence.

terminology.meaning: Hypothetical AI with human-level general cognitive ability across arbitrary tasks, as opposed to narrow task-specific systems.
Hypothetical AI far surpassing human capabilities in general.

connections: p.600: chapter 19 revisits why 'intelligence' in 'artificial intelligence' has been a category error.

paragraphs.excerpt: It might be tempting for those new to the field to assume
paragraphs.what_it_says: Newcomers assume that generative AI's successes caused the belief in near-term AGI; the authors say the causality runs the other way. In 2013 tech elites already feared that DeepMind (London, later acquired by Google) was near AGI. That fear motivated the founding of OpenAI in 2015 as an open-source counterweight; OpenAI then kick-started generative AI. In 2016 OpenAI's recruiting pitch promised AGI by 2020. Few believed such timelines then; by early 2023 a significant fraction of San Francisco Bay Area engineers expected AGI within a couple of years.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The belief in imminent AGI is an old, recurring narrative that *preceded* the technology it is now attached to. The institutional history (DeepMind fear → OpenAI founding → generative-AI breakthroughs) shows that the expectation shaped the field's investments rather than being an inference from results. The 2016 'AGI by 2020' pitch is given as a concrete example of a confident timeline that did not come true.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Knowing that the AGI timeline was already 'a few years away' in 2013 and in 2016 helps the reader calibrate the identical claims heard in 2023. It is the same move the authors make on p.38 with Minsky's 1967 and 1970 predictions.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (inference, not in the book): the argument is a causal one about social history — a belief (B) produced institutions (OpenAI) that produced a technology (generative AI); observers who see only B and the technology together wrongly infer technology → B.

terminology.meaning: London AI research startup acquired by Google; in 2013 some feared it was on track to AGI.
Founded in 2015, initially as an open-source counterweight to DeepMind; played a critical role in kick-starting generative AI.

connections: p.35: section 1.8 'The age of generative AI' describes the wave that OpenAI helped start.
p.38: Minsky's 1967/1970 AGI predictions — the same over-optimism in an earlier era.

paragraphs.excerpt: It’s crucial to approach such claims with a healthy dose of skepticism.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Such claims deserve skepticism. Despite its name, today's AI is more accurately 'cognitive automation': the encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge. AI excels at problems with narrowly defined requirements or ample precise examples. It enhances computers' capabilities; it does not replicate human minds.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The authors propose a more accurate label. 'Cognitive automation' captures what deep learning actually does: it takes skills and knowledge that humans already have (expressed as examples or rules) and turns them into executable machinery. The two conditions under which it excels — narrow requirements, or many precise examples — are exactly the conditions under which the mapping from inputs to outputs can be learned or specified in full.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This reframing is the conceptual core of the page and of chapter 19 (p.600, where the authors say the 'intelligence' label has been a category error). It tells you what to expect from the models you will build in this book: they operationalize skills from data, they do not think.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: 'ample precise examples' corresponds to the dense sampling of input–output pairs that supervised deep learning needs; chapter 19 (p.600) describes this as *local generalization* — a learned smooth mapping from space X to Y that breaks when inputs drift away from the training distribution.

terminology.meaning: The encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge in a machine — the authors' preferred description of today's AI.

connections: p.600: 'It would be more accurate to call our field artificial cognition, with cognitive automation and artificial intelligence being two nearly independent subfields.'
p.603: human-like intelligence is not skill at a particular task but the ability to adapt to novelty and acquire new skills efficiently.

paragraphs.excerpt: To be clear, cognitive automation is incredibly useful. But intelligence
paragraphs.what_it_says: Cognitive automation is incredibly useful, but intelligence — cognitive *autonomy* — is a different creature. Analogy: AI is like a cartoon character, intelligence like a living being. A cartoon, however realistic, can only act out the scenes it was drawn for; a living being can adapt to the unexpected.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The contrast is automation vs. autonomy. A cartoon's apparent behaviour is entirely authored in advance (by the animator; for a model, by the training data and the training procedure). Nothing in it can respond to a situation that was not drawn. A living being has an internal capacity to generate new behaviour for new circumstances.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The analogy gives the reader a concrete mental test: ask not 'how convincing is the output?' but 'what happens in a situation that was never in the training distribution?'

terminology.meaning: The authors' gloss on intelligence: the capacity to act appropriately in situations not prepared for in advance.

connections: p.600: 'Early AI systems were pure automatons, like the ELIZA chat program' — the automaton theme in chapter 19.

paragraphs.excerpt: “If the cartoon is drawn with sufficient realism and covers sufficiently many scenes
paragraphs.what_it_says: The authors raise the natural objection — if the cartoon is realistic enough and covers enough scenes, what's the difference? If an LLM gives a sufficiently human-sounding answer, does it matter whether it has cognitive autonomy? — and answer: the key difference is adaptability. Intelligence is the ability to face the unknown, adapt to it and learn from it. Automation, even at its best, only handles situations it has been trained on or programmed for; that is why robust automation is so hard — every possible scenario must be accounted for.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the operational definition of intelligence the book uses: *adaptation to novelty*, not quality of output on known cases. It also explains an engineering fact: the long tail of rare situations is what makes automation brittle, because an automated system must have each situation covered in advance, whereas an intelligent agent covers them on the fly.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It answers the strongest form of the AGI argument ('scale the coverage and the distinction vanishes') and it foreshadows the book's later discussion of why scale alone is not enough (p.597, section 19.2) and of benchmarks like ARC-AGI that test adaptation to never-seen tasks (p.607–608).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in machine-learning terms, 'covering enough scenes' means expanding the training distribution; 'facing the unknown' means out-of-distribution generalization. The authors' claim is that no finite expansion of the former yields the latter.

terminology.meaning: The capacity to handle, and learn from, situations not seen before — the authors' criterion separating intelligence from automation.

connections: p.597: section 19.2 'Scale isn't all you need' develops why adding coverage is not the same as adding intelligence.
p.607: ARC-AGI results — a system can solve many tasks at huge compute cost yet still be stumped by tasks humans find easy.

paragraphs.excerpt: So don’t worry about AI suddenly becoming self-aware and taking over humanity.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Conclusion: don't worry about AI suddenly becoming self-aware and taking over; today's technology is not headed in that direction. The sentence continues on p.38: even with significant advancements, AI will remain a sophisticated tool, not a sentient being — like expecting a better clock to lead to time travel.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Because current systems are automation rather than autonomy, improvements along the current axis (more data, bigger models, better coverage) make a better tool, not a different kind of thing. The clock/time-travel image on p.38 makes the category difference vivid.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It states the authors' position plainly so the reader can hold a balanced view while reading the rest of the book: practical optimism about what deep learning can do, skepticism about claims that it is on the verge of becoming a mind.
connections: p.38: the clock vs. time travel comparison that completes this sentence.
p.39: 'Don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision.'

concepts.name: Cognitive automation
concepts.definition: The encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge in a computer system — the authors' more accurate name for what today's 'artificial intelligence' does.
concepts.intuition: A deep learning model is like a very flexible recording of human know-how: it replays, on new inputs, skills that were present in its training examples.
concepts.technical: Deep learning automates tasks from exposure to data: given ample precise examples (or narrowly defined requirements), a model learns a mapping from inputs to outputs that reproduces the demonstrated skill. It works best precisely where the task can be fully specified by examples.
concepts.significance: Reframing AI as cognitive automation explains both its enormous practical value (every industry has skills worth automating) and its limits (it does not replicate minds).
concepts.example: Image classification, speech transcription, machine translation and chatbot answers — all items of the p.35–36 list — are human skills encoded from large example sets.
concepts.misconception: That a system which performs a human skill at human level must therefore possess human-like intelligence. The authors argue skill at a fixed task says nothing about adaptability.

concepts.name: Intelligence as adaptability (cognitive autonomy)
concepts.definition: The ability to face the unknown, adapt to it, and learn from it; contrasted with automation, which can only handle situations it was trained on or programmed for.
concepts.intuition: A living being can cope with a scene nobody drew in advance; a cartoon cannot.
concepts.technical: Operationally, the criterion is behaviour on situations outside the training/programming coverage. Automation requires every scenario to be accounted for beforehand; intelligence generates appropriate behaviour for new scenarios on the fly.
concepts.significance: It is the yardstick the authors use to judge claims of AGI and, in chapter 19, to design benchmarks (ARC-AGI) that measure adaptation rather than memorized skill.
concepts.example: An LLM that answers familiar questions fluently may still fail on a genuinely novel puzzle; the fluency measures coverage, not autonomy.
concepts.misconception: That sufficiently realistic output is equivalent to intelligence. The authors answer the 'sufficiently many scenes' objection directly: the difference is adaptability, not realism.

concepts.name: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) hype
concepts.definition: The claim that human-level general intelligence — or a superintelligence beyond humans — is about to arrive.
concepts.intuition: A recurring prediction that is always 'a few years away': 2013 (DeepMind), 2016 (OpenAI's 'AGI by 2020'), early 2023 (Bay Area engineers).
concepts.technical: The authors treat it as the most sensational layer of AI hype and argue that current technology — cognitive automation — is not headed toward autonomy at all.
concepts.significance: Belief in near-term AGI shaped the field institutionally: it motivated OpenAI's founding (2015), which in turn kick-started generative AI.
concepts.example: OpenAI's 2016 recruiting pitch promised AGI by 2020.
concepts.misconception: That generative AI's success is what created the belief in imminent AGI. The book says the belief came first and fuelled generative AI.

concepts.name: Short-term hype
concepts.definition: Inflated near-term expectations about a technology, here AI, that outrun its actual delivered impact.
concepts.intuition: Promises of 100× productivity and imminent AGI versus an economic impact that so far 'pales in comparison'.
concepts.technical: Section 1.10 distinguishes economic hype (unemployment, productivity) from the stronger AGI/superintelligence hype; section 1.11 (p.38) explains the historical consequence — AI winters.
concepts.significance: Recognizing hype lets practitioners keep realistic expectations and protects the field from the funding collapses that followed earlier over-promising.
concepts.example: Minsky's 1970 prediction of human-level general intelligence 'in from three to eight years' (p.38).
concepts.misconception: That skepticism about hype means pessimism about AI. The authors are optimistic about the long term (p.39) while skeptical about short-term claims.

deeper.title: The causal chain the authors describe
deeper.body:
The page's historical argument, laid out as a sequence (all dates are from the page):

1. **2013** — Tech elites fear that DeepMind (London; acquired by Google) may reach AGI within a few years.
2. **2015** — That fear is the impetus for founding OpenAI, initially meant as an open-source counterweight to DeepMind.
3. **2016** — OpenAI's recruiting pitch: AGI by 2020. Only a minority in the industry believe the timeline.
4. **2022 onward** (p.35–36) — OpenAI plays a critical role in kick-starting the generative-AI wave.
5. **Early 2023** — A significant fraction of Bay Area engineers expect AGI within a couple of years.

The 'peculiar twist': belief in AGI (step 1) is upstream of generative AI (step 4). A newcomer who first sees steps 4 and 5 naturally but wrongly infers that 4 caused 5's belief.

deeper.title: Cartoon vs. living being, in machine-learning terms
deeper.body:
The authors' analogy maps neatly onto training-distribution language (this mapping is mine, not the book's):

| Cartoon | Deep learning model |
|---|---|
| Scenes the animator drew | Situations represented in the training data |
| Realism of the drawing | Quality of outputs on in-distribution inputs |
| Drawing more scenes | Collecting more data / scaling the model |
| A scene nobody drew | An out-of-distribution input |
| Living being adapting | Learning something new at the moment it is needed |

The objection 'draw enough scenes and there is no difference' is the scaling hypothesis; the authors' reply is that the unknown is, by definition, the set of scenes that were *not* drawn, and no amount of drawing makes that set empty. That is also why robust automation is so hard: the engineer, like the animator, has to anticipate everything.

deeper.title: Why 'narrowly defined requirements or ample precise examples' are the sweet spot
deeper.body:
The page says AI excels at two kinds of problems. Both are cases where the task can be fully specified in advance (an explanation that goes beyond the book):

- **Narrowly defined requirements**: the input and output spaces are small and well understood (e.g. classify a 28×28 digit into 10 classes), so the mapping can be captured without surprises.
- **Ample precise examples**: even if the task is hard to write down as rules (translation, image captioning), a dense enough sample of correct input–output pairs lets a model interpolate between them.

What both exclude is the case where the right behaviour must be *invented* for a situation absent from both the specification and the examples — which is exactly the 'face the unknown' capacity the page reserves for intelligence. Chapter 19 (p.600) calls what models currently do *local generalization*.

misconceptions.claim: Generative AI's practical successes are what made people believe AGI is near.
misconceptions.correction: The page says the opposite: belief in near-term AGI (from 2013) motivated OpenAI's founding in 2015, and OpenAI then helped kick-start generative AI. The belief fuelled the technology, not the other way around.

misconceptions.claim: If a model's answers are indistinguishable from a human's, it must be intelligent.
misconceptions.correction: The authors argue that the distinguishing property is adaptability to the unknown, not realism of output on known situations. A cartoon can be arbitrarily realistic and still only act out drawn scenes.

misconceptions.claim: Calling today's AI 'cognitive automation' belittles it.
misconceptions.correction: The authors explicitly say cognitive automation is 'incredibly useful' and that AI 'excels' at narrowly defined problems and problems with ample examples. The label is about accuracy, not dismissal.

misconceptions.claim: With enough advances, current AI will become self-aware.
misconceptions.correction: The page says today's technology 'simply isn't headed in that direction'; p.38 completes the thought — a better tool stays a tool, like a better clock not leading to time travel.

prerequisites.note: What machine learning is (learning rules from data), the basis of 'operationalizing skills from examples'.

takeaways: The belief in imminent AGI predates generative AI: 2013 fears about DeepMind led to OpenAI's founding in 2015, and OpenAI then kick-started generative AI.
Confident AGI timelines have a track record of failing — e.g. OpenAI's 2016 pitch of AGI by 2020 — so claims heard in 2023 deserve skepticism.
Today's AI is best described as cognitive automation: the encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge, excelling at narrow problems or those with ample precise examples.
Intelligence is cognitive autonomy — the ability to face the unknown, adapt and learn — whereas automation only handles situations it was trained or programmed for.
Realism of output is not the test: a cartoon can be arbitrarily realistic yet only act out drawn scenes; the test is adaptability.
Robust automation is hard precisely because every possible scenario has to be accounted for in advance.
Current technology is not headed toward self-awareness; improvements make a better tool, not a sentient being.

questions.question: According to the authors, what is the relationship between belief in near-term AGI and the rise of generative AI?
options: Generative AI's successes created the belief in near-term AGI.
Belief in near-term AGI came first and contributed to the rise of generative AI.
The two are unrelated phenomena that happened to coincide.
Belief in AGI only emerged after ChatGPT was released in 2022.
questions.answer: Belief in near-term AGI came first and contributed to the rise of generative AI.
questions.explanation: The page says newcomers' assumption (first option) is 'actually backward': fears about DeepMind in 2013 motivated the founding of OpenAI in 2015, and OpenAI kick-started generative AI. They are causally linked, so 'unrelated' is wrong, and the belief dates to 2013, not 2022.

questions.question: What term do the authors propose as a more accurate description of today's 'artificial intelligence', and how do they define it?
questions.answer: Cognitive automation — the encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge.
questions.explanation: The page states that despite its name, today's AI is 'more accurately described as cognitive automation — the encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge'. It enhances computers' capabilities rather than replicating human minds.

questions.question: Explain the cartoon-character vs. living-being analogy and how the authors respond to the objection 'if the cartoon covers enough scenes, what's the difference?'
questions.answer: A cartoon, however realistic, can only act out the scenes it was drawn for; a living being can adapt to the unexpected. The authors answer the objection by saying the key difference is adaptability: intelligence is the ability to face the unknown, adapt to it and learn from it, whereas automation can only handle situations it has been trained on or programmed for.
questions.explanation: The analogy equates AI with the cartoon (behaviour fully authored in advance) and intelligence with the living being (behaviour generated for new situations). The objection assumes coverage can substitute for autonomy; the authors reply that the unknown is precisely what was not covered, so no amount of realism closes the gap.

questions.question: Which two kinds of problems does the page say AI excels at?
options: Problems with narrowly defined requirements, or problems where ample precise examples are available
Problems requiring common sense, or problems never seen before
Problems with no training data, or problems defined only in natural language
Problems that humans find hard, or problems requiring self-awareness
questions.answer: Problems with narrowly defined requirements, or problems where ample precise examples are available
questions.explanation: The page: 'AI excels at solving problems with narrowly defined requirements or those where ample precise examples are available.' The other options describe exactly the kind of novelty the page says automation cannot handle.

questions.question: What did OpenAI's 2016 recruiting pitch promise, and why do the authors mention it?
questions.answer: That OpenAI would achieve AGI by 2020. It is cited as an example of an over-optimistic AGI timeline that did not come true, to encourage skepticism about similar claims made in 2023.
questions.explanation: The page says 'In 2016, OpenAI's recruiting pitch was that it would achieve AGI by 2020!' and then notes that by early 2023 many engineers again believed AGI was a couple of years away, urging 'a healthy dose of skepticism'.

questions.question: Why, according to the page, is creating robust automation so challenging?
questions.answer: Because automation can only handle situations it has been trained on or programmed for, so building robust automation requires accounting for every possible scenario in advance.
questions.explanation: This follows directly from the automation/intelligence distinction: an automated system lacks the ability to adapt to the unknown, so its designers must anticipate the full range of situations it will encounter.

questions.question: Think of an AI product you use. In the authors' terms, which 'scenes' was it drawn for (what skill was encoded from what examples), and can you describe a realistic situation outside those scenes where you would expect it to fail?
questions.answer: Open-ended. A good answer names the human skill being automated, the kind of data it was learned from, and a concrete out-of-coverage situation (new domain, unusual input, a task requiring invention rather than recall).
questions.explanation: This exercises the page's criterion: judge a system by its behaviour on the unknown, not by the realism of its output on familiar inputs.
